title: Cyperus digitatus: How to Spot and Control Finger Flatsedge in Rice
metaTitle: Cyperus digitatus: Finger Flatsedge in Rice Fields
metaDescription: Cyperus digitatus, or finger flatsedge, grows in lowland rice. See how to spot its yellow spikes and how to dig it out with its rhizomes for good.
excerpt: Cyperus digitatus, or finger flatsedge, is a sedge weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. It can live for more than one season and spreads by seed and by underground stems. This page shows how to spot its yellow, finger like flower spikes and how to control it in your palay.

heroImage.alt: Finger flatsedge (Cyperus digitatus), a sedge weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family. Its English name, finger flatsedge, comes from the way its flower spikes spread out like the fingers of a hand. PhilRice's weed list gives no Filipino local name for it. So this page uses its scientific name, Cyperus digitatus. You will see it in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields.

It is usually a perennial, but some plants live for one season only. It spreads in two ways. First, its flowers make seeds that fall into the soil. Second, it grows rhizomes, which are stems that creep under the ground and send up new shoots. Because of these rhizomes, an old clump can come back in the same spot after you cut it.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Cyperus digitatus
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like other sedges, it has a solid, triangular stem with no nodes. You can feel the three edges when you roll the stem between your fingers. Its leaves are flat. At the top, it carries a compound flower head, and its spikes spread out from one point like the fingers of a hand. The spikelets are yellow, so the heads stand out against green palay leaves.

items: A solid stem with three clear edges and no joints along its length.
Flat leaves rising from the base of the plant.
A branched flower head whose spikes fan out like fingers from one point.
Yellow spikelets that look bright against the green rice leaves.
New shoots coming up close to an old clump, a sign of rhizomes below.

blocks.text:
Like most sedges, Cyperus digitatus competes with palay for light, water and fertilizer. Because it can live for more than one season, an old clump keeps drawing on your soil crop after crop. Its rhizomes also let each patch grow wider over time, so the space left for rice keeps shrinking.

When it flowers, its seeds can end up in harvested palay and lower the quality of seed you keep. Dense clumps also give rats and insect pests a place to hide close to the rice hills. So it pays to remove it while patches are still small.

items: Dig out each clump with its rhizomes, because pieces left in the soil can grow into new plants.
After plowing, gather rhizome pieces that come to the surface and dry them in the sun, away from the paddy.
Pull or cut plants before the yellow spikelets ripen, so no new seed falls into the field.
Keep bunds and canal edges clean, since perennial clumps there can creep back into the paddy.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold Cyperus digitatus down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Cyperus digitatus Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Cyperus digitatus

items.q: What is the common name of Cyperus digitatus?
items.a: In English it goes by finger flatsedge, because its spikes spread out like fingers. PhilRice's weed list gives no Filipino local name for it. So when you ask a technician about it, use the English or scientific name. You can also show a photo of its yellow, finger like flower heads.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Begin with clean seed and a well leveled field with steady water. Then dig out clumps by hand, rhizomes and all, before they flower. Since it can regrow from below, check the same spots again after a few weeks. If you need a herbicide, choose one for sedges that fits your rice age. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does finger flatsedge come back in the same spot?
items.a: It comes back because it is usually a perennial with rhizomes under the soil. When you cut only the top, those rhizomes stay alive and send up new shoots. Seeds that fell in earlier seasons can sprout as well. To stop it, dig out the whole clump with its rhizomes and remove the plants before they seed.
